difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY - one concept (evaluating a tuple relational calculus query with existential quantifiers) on a three-row relation; once the z-clause is seen to be always true, it is a single S > 1 check per tuple, about 1 to 1.5 minutes.
stem:
Let there be two relations $X$ and $Y$ as shown. $X$ has three columns $P$, $Q$ and $R$. $Y$ has two columns $P$ and $S$.

$X$

| $P$ | $Q$ | $R$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| P1 | Q1 | R1 |
| P2 | Q2 | R2 |
| P3 | Q3 | R2 |

$Y$

| $P$ | $S$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| P1 | 10 |
| P1 | 15 |
| P2 | 20 |
| P3 | 1 |

Consider that the following tuple relational calculus expression is evaluated.

$$
\{t \mid t \in X \land \exists z \in X(t[P] = z[P]) \land \exists m \in Y\,(m[P] = t[P] \land m[S] > 1)\}
$$

The number of tuples that will be returned is __________ . (Answer in **integer**)

solution.quick: The clause $\exists z \in X\,(t[P] = z[P])$ is always true (take $z = t$), so the query returns the tuples $t$ of $X$ whose $P$ value has at least one row in $Y$ with $S > 1$. P1 (with $S$ = 10, 15) and P2 ($S$ = 20) qualify; P3's only row has $S = 1$, and $1 > 1$ is false. Result: (P1, Q1, R1) and (P2, Q2, R2), i.e. **2** tuples.

steps.title: Read the query
steps.body:
In tuple relational calculus, $\{t \mid F(t)\}$ returns every tuple $t$ for which the formula $F(t)$ is true. Here $F$ is a conjunction of three conditions:

1. $t \in X$: the answer tuples are rows of $X$ (columns $P, Q, R$), so at most 3 tuples can be returned.
2. $\exists z \in X\,(t[P] = z[P])$: some row $z$ of $X$ has the same $P$ value as $t$.
3. $\exists m \in Y\,(m[P] = t[P] \land m[S] > 1)$: some row $m$ of $Y$ has the same $P$ value as $t$ **and** an $S$ value strictly greater than 1.

steps.title: The second condition is always true
steps.body: Since $t$ itself is a row of $X$, choose $z = t$; then $t[P] = z[P]$ holds trivially. So condition 2 is satisfied by every $t \in X$ and removes nothing. The only real filter is condition 3.

steps.title: Check the third condition for each tuple of X
Count the result
steps.body:
The expression returns $\{(\text{P1}, \text{Q1}, \text{R1}),\ (\text{P2}, \text{Q2}, \text{R2})\}$.

P1 has two qualifying rows in $Y$, but the existential quantifier only asks whether *at least one* such row exists. The output tuple is $t$ itself, a row of $X$, so (P1, Q1, R1) appears once. The number of tuples returned is **2**.

In relational algebra the same query is the semi-join $X \ltimes \sigma_{S > 1}(Y)$, or equivalently $\Pi_{P,Q,R}\big(X \bowtie \sigma_{S > 1}(Y)\big)$ under set semantics.

The official key accepts any value from 2 to 3; the evaluation above gives exactly 2.

solution.teaching:
**What a TRC query says.** A tuple relational calculus query $\{t \mid F(t)\}$ is declarative: it describes *which* tuples belong to the answer, not how to compute them. $t$ is a tuple variable; a condition like $t \in X$ ties it to the rows of relation $X$, and $t[P]$ means the value of attribute $P$ in $t$.

**Existential quantifiers are yes/no tests.** $\exists m \in Y\,(\ldots)$ reads "there is at least one row $m$ of $Y$ such that ...". For the current $t$ it is simply true or false: it adds no columns to the output and does not create one output row per matching $m$. That is the key difference from a join. The join $X \bowtie Y$ pairs $t$ with every matching $m$ and can produce several rows for one $t$; an existential condition only keeps or drops $t$. In relational algebra this pattern is the **semi-join** $X \ltimes Y$, or a join followed by a projection back onto $X$'s columns, which removes duplicates under set semantics.

**Spotting redundant conditions.** A condition such as $\exists z \in X\,(t[P] = z[P])$ together with $t \in X$ is always satisfied, because $t$ itself is a witness. Recognising such tautologies saves time.

**Evaluating a TRC query by hand.** Go through the candidate tuples (here the rows of $X$) one at a time. For each existential condition, search the other relation for a witness row. Keep $t$ only if every condition has a witness. Watch strict versus non-strict comparisons ($>$ versus $\ge$) and values that sit exactly on the boundary.

**Connecting to this question.** For each of the 3 rows of $X$ we need a row of $Y$ with the same $P$ and $S > 1$. P1 and P2 have such witnesses; P3's only row has $S = 1$, which fails the strict test. So 2 tuples are returned.
solution.shortcut: Drop the tautological $\exists z$ clause (take $z = t$). Then, for each $P$ value of $X$, ask whether $Y$ has a row with that $P$ and $S > 1$: P1 yes, P2 yes, P3 no (its only $S$ is 1). Answer: 2.
solution.commonTrap: Counting the rows of the join $X \bowtie \sigma_{S > 1}(Y)$ instead of the tuples of $X$: P1 matches two rows of $Y$, which gives 3 join rows, but the output tuples are the $t \in X$ and the existential quantifier keeps (P1, Q1, R1) only once. Other slips: reading $m[S] > 1$ as $m[S] \ge 1$, which wrongly keeps P3, or thinking the $\exists z$ clause filters something out.

transcription.notes: Single-pass transcription from the official paper rendering; awaiting independent check. In the paper the relations X and Y are printed side by side, each captioned with its italic name; they are transcribed as two GFM tables, one after the other, with the cells centred as printed. The column headers P, Q, R, S are in math italics in the paper and are rendered as math; the cell values (P1, Q1, R1, ..., 10, 15, 20, 1) are upright and kept as plain text. The TRC expression is transcribed with \land for the conjunction symbol and \exists for the existential quantifier. The paper prints no space between X and the parenthesis in the first quantifier but a space before the parenthesis in the second; a thin space is used for the second, which is typographic only. 'integer' is bold in the answer note, as in the paper, and the space the paper leaves between the answer blank and the full stop is kept. The region has no embedded figure and none is needed.

answerVerification.checkCode:
X = [('P1', 'Q1', 'R1'), ('P2', 'Q2', 'R2'), ('P3', 'Q3', 'R2')]   # (P, Q, R)
Y = [('P1', 10), ('P1', 15), ('P2', 20), ('P3', 1)]                # (P, S)
P, S = 0, 1
# {t | t in X and (exists z in X: t[P]=z[P]) and (exists m in Y: m[P]=t[P] and m[S]>1)}
result = {t for t in X
          if any(t[P] == z[P] for z in X)
          and any(m[P] == t[P] and m[S] > 1 for m in Y)}
print(sorted(result), len(result))          # [('P1','Q1','R1'), ('P2','Q2','R2')] 2
assert len(result) == 2
assert all(any(t[P] == z[P] for z in X) for t in X)   # the z-clause is always true (take z = t)
# contrast: rows of the join X |><| sigma_{S>1}(Y) before projecting back onto X
join_rows = [(t, m) for t in X for m in Y if m[P] == t[P] and m[S] > 1]
print('join rows', len(join_rows))        # 3 (P1 matches two Y rows)
# contrast: with S >= 1 instead of S > 1, P3 would also qualify
assert len({t for t in X if any(m[P] == t[P] and m[S] >= 1 for m in Y)}) == 3
assert 2 <= len(result) <= 3              # official key 2 to 3
answerVerification.notes: Evaluating the TRC expression literally in Python over the transcribed relations returns {(P1, Q1, R1), (P2, Q2, R2)}, i.e. 2 tuples. The z-clause holds for every t in X (take z = t), and P3 is excluded because its only Y row has S = 1, which fails S > 1. The official key is the range 2 to 3, which contains the derived value 2; the key range also admits 3, but the expression as printed evaluates to exactly 2.
